title: Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel
content:
Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel
This article surveys the life and the immense Torah contribution of Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel, a unique figure who served as a connecting link between the meticulous world of the Lithuanian yeshivot and the world of thought and Kabbalah of Religious Zionism. The text details his groundbreaking methodology, the "method of treasuries," designed to make the richness of Jewish thought and the complex teaching of Rav Kook accessible through thematic organization, broad bibliographic mapping and clear explanations. Beyond his extensive literary enterprise, the article highlights the rabbi's moral and ascetic personality as a model to emulate, while presenting his worldview, which combined tremendous diligence in Torah, simple faith in the wonders of Creation and firm Jewish nationalism. The aim of the survey is to illustrate how the rabbi succeeded in turning scattered Torah knowledge into an orderly and accessible body of teaching, and thereby in passing on the "soul of the Torah" to the present generation of learners.
The Torah Enterprise and Thought of Faith of Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel: A Comprehensive Study of His Figure, Writings and Influence
The Torah enterprise of Rabbi Moshe Yechiel Tzuriel, of blessed memory (5698–5783), represents a rare phenomenon in the rabbinic landscape of the twentieth century and the beginning of the twenty-first, for it combines three skills that often do not dwell together: encyclopedic, wide-ranging erudition in all the treasures of the Torah, an ability for organization and bibliography at a scholarly level, and profound thought of faith connected to the inner dimension of the Torah and to the teaching of Rav Kook.[1, 2] In the eyes of his students and colleagues, Rabbi Tzuriel appeared as a kind of "living bridge" between the conservative and precise world of Lithuanian learning, in which he grew up in Bnei Brak, and the complex world of Religious-Zionist and kabbalistic thought, in which he found his spiritual home.[2] Over more than sixty years of creative work, Rabbi Tzuriel produced a vast literary corpus comprising dozens of volumes, the hallmark of his writing being the genre of "treasuries" (otzrot): thematic anthologies that present the words of the great sages of Israel in an orderly, indexed and annotated form, giving the modern learner quick access to the depths of Jewish thought.[1, 3]
Chapter 1: Stations of Life and the Shaping of a Spiritual Identity
Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel's development was marked by a multidimensional encounter with the central Torah centers of the generation of national revival. He immigrated to Israel in 1956 and chose to make his place of study at Yeshivat Mercaz HaRav, where he absorbed the first foundations of the Torah of the Land of Israel.[2] During that period, Rabbi Tzuriel formed a direct connection with the yeshiva's spiritual leadership, studying twice a week in a study partnership (chavruta) with Rabbi Eliezer Waldman under the close guidance of Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda Kook.[2] At the same time, he attended the classes of "the Nazir," Rabbi David Cohen, a figure who profoundly influenced his attachment to the hidden realm and to the link between philosophy and Kabbalah.[2]
After a short period of study abroad to complete an academic degree, a step that reflected his intellectual openness and his wish to become acquainted with the tools of Western scholarship, Rabbi Tzuriel returned to Israel in 1960 and resumed his studies at Yeshivat Mercaz HaRav.[2] However, his broad and profound Torah education in the "revealed" Torah was shaped to a great extent by his studies at the Chazon Ish Kollel in Bnei Brak, from 1961 onward.[2] There, in the stronghold of Lithuanian scholarship, he studied alongside outstanding Torah giants such as Rabbi Gedalia Nadel, Rabbi Nissim Karelitz and Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky.[2] The influence of the kollel was evident in the rabbi's ability for textual precision and in his uncompromising fidelity to the sources of the Rishonim and Acharonim, a quality that accompanied him in all his later anthological enterprises.[2]
Rabbi Tzuriel's teaching career was varied and spread a broad network of influence over different audiences. He began his path in secondary education in Hadera and Bnei Brak, an experience that enabled him to understand the need to make the Torah accessible to a public not versed in classical yeshiva study.[2] In 1977 he began serving as mashgiach (spiritual supervisor) at the Sha'alvim hesder yeshiva, a position he held for 18 years.[2] During this period his figure took shape as a spiritual guide and a man of mussar, combining a demand for the refinement of character traits with in-depth study of the aggadot of the Sages and the writings of Rav Kook.[2, 4] In his last years he taught at Yeshivat Torat HaChaim, both when it was in Gush Katif and after its move to Yad Binyamin, as well as at the hesder yeshiva in Rishon LeZion, where he continued to pass on his unique method of study.[2, 4]
Milestones and Dates in the Biography of Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel
Chapter 2: The Methodology of the "Treasuries": A Revolution in Torah Bibliography
The central task that Rabbi Tzuriel took upon himself was the reorganization of Torah knowledge scattered across hundreds of books, out of an understanding that the contemporary learner needs aids that will allow him to encompass entire subjects without getting lost in the sea of sources.[3, 6] This method, known as the "method of treasuries," rests on three core principles: comprehensive collection from all the generations of Torah, precise thematic arrangement, and the addition of short explanations that clarify the difficult points.[1, 3]
Rabbi Tzuriel did not see himself merely as a technical anthologist. His work required a phenomenal memory and an ability to identify conceptual connections between texts from different periods.[2] His son, Rabbi Avraham Tzuriel, described how "the whole Torah lay in the palm of his hand," and how his father was able to pull out any book and open it at exactly the page needed to prove a point or bring a complementary source.[2] This ability enabled him to create thematic indexes without equal, such as "Leket Mafteḥot Sifrei Yesod" (A Collection of Indexes to Foundational Books), which covers 26 foundational books of faith and thought.[1]
The influence of his methodology is especially evident in the field of the aggadot of the Talmud. In the four-volume series "Leket Perushei Aggadah" (A Collection of Commentaries on Aggadah), Rabbi Tzuriel gathered commentaries from more than 120 different books, adding his own explanations to them.[1] This work counteracted the modern tendency to interpret aggadah according to personal logic alone, and brought the learner back to the interpretive tradition of the great sages of the generations.[7] Rabbi Harel Dvir noted that the rabbi's classes on the aggadot of the Sages were a center of attraction for students, owing to their combination of command of the sources with topical moral insights.[5]
Chapter 3: The "Otzrot HaRe'iyah" Enterprise: Making Rav Kook's Teaching Accessible
Rabbi Tzuriel's most distinctive contribution to the world of Religious-Zionist thought is the series "Otzrot HaRe'iyah" (Treasures of Rav Kook). The writings of Rav Kook are known for their linguistic complexity and for being scattered across many books, essays, letters and manuscripts.[6] Rabbi Tzuriel recognized that without a deep thematic index, Rav Kook's teaching might remain the possession of a select few alone.[6]
The "Otzrot HaRe'iyah" series, comprising seven volumes, is far more than a technical index. It contains five main parts: the life of the rabbi and testimonies about him, explanations of his system arranged by subject, selected quotations ("sparks"), annotated letters, and bibliographic appendices.[8] In the sixth and seventh volumes, which were published in later years (around 5775), Rabbi Tzuriel expanded the scope of the work and included new essays not yet printed, halakhic responsa from manuscripts, and indexes to books that have appeared in recent decades, such as "Pinkesei HaRe'iyah" (Rav Kook's Notebooks) and "LiNevukhei HaDor" (For the Perplexed of the Generation).[6]
His methodology in "Otzrot HaRe'iyah" developed over the years. Whereas in the early editions he noted "mentions" of subjects, in the later editions he concentrated on the places where Rav Kook interpreted the subject in depth.[6] This approach required a critical and thorough reading of all of Rav Kook's writings, distinguishing between a passing remark and a systematic principle.[6] In addition, Rabbi Tzuriel included in the series essays by other Torah giants explaining Rav Kook's teaching, thereby creating an "encyclopedia of Rav Kook's teaching" encompassing every aspect of his life and thought.[6]
Structure and Arrangement of the "Otzrot HaRe'iyah" Series (Expanded Edition)
Chapter 4: The Teaching of Mussar and Holy Conduct
Rabbi Tzuriel was not content with theoretical study alone; he saw the study of mussar as the essence of everything.[1, 9] In the series "Otzrot HaMussar" (two volumes), he collected words of thought and opinion from dozens of mussar books of the Rishonim and Acharonim, focusing on the refinement of character traits and the attainment of pure faith.[9] One of the unique parts of this series is "Otzar Avodat Hashem" (A Treasury of the Service of God), a work written on the model of "Sefer Haredim" by Rabbi Elazar Azikri, which deals with the sanctity of the limbs and the commandments associated with them.[1, 9]
Rabbi Tzuriel's moral thought was characterized by a straight and uncompromising line in the search for truth. He stressed the importance of separation from the ways of the gentiles and from foreign influences, a theme expressed in his book "Hen Am Levadad Yishkon" (Lo, It Is a People That Shall Dwell Alone).[1] At the same time, he called for national pride and boundless love of Israel, combining Haredi fear of Heaven with Religious-Zionist activism.[2, 7]
The rabbi's personality served as a living model of his moral teaching. He was known for his tremendous diligence, taking care to pray at sunrise for more than 60 years.[2] His students described him as an "angel" withdrawn from the affairs of this world, a man who ate only the minimum needed to fulfill the commandments and lived in extreme modesty in his home on Beit Hillel Street in Bnei Brak.[2, 10] For many decades Rabbi Tzuriel refused to accept payment for his classes, out of the conviction that the study and dissemination of Torah must be done solely for its own sake.[2]
Chapter 5: "Nifla'im Ma'asekha": The Link Between Faith and Nature
One of Rabbi Tzuriel's most fascinating and popular works is the book "Nifla'im Ma'asekha" (Wondrous Are Your Works). In this work, Rabbi Tzuriel goes beyond the bounds of the classical beit midrash and dives into the wonders of Creation and the physiology of the human body.[1] The aim of the book is to show how the governance of nature testifies to the wisdom of the Creator, and thereby to strengthen the learner's faith through contemplation of tangible reality.[1]
This approach reflects a broad theological conception found in the writings of Rav Kook and the Maharal, according to which there is no disconnect between the spiritual world and the material world. Rabbi Tzuriel used scientific knowledge (based on the sources of the Sages and on general knowledge) to illustrate divine providence.[1] The book became an important educational tool for teachers and rabbis seeking to instill faith in the young in a generation of rational inquiry.[1]
In addition to his engagement with nature, Rabbi Tzuriel devoted great attention to the Masorah and to biblical grammar. In the series "Masoret Seyag LaTorah" (The Masorah Is a Fence for the Torah; three volumes), he examined words in Scripture whose spelling is distinctive according to the Masorah.[1] He saw biblical grammar not merely as a technical field but as a spiritual "code" concealing profound ideas, as also emerges from his book "Or HaTorah," which deals with the methods of gematria.[1]
Chapter 6: The Editing Project: Reviving the Writings of the Kabbalists and the Rishonim
A less well-known but significant side of Rabbi Tzuriel's enterprise is his work as an editor of ancient books. The rabbi attached supreme importance to publishing rare books, or books written in difficult language, while making them accessible to the general public.[1] He devoted great efforts to the writings of Rabbi Moshe Cordovero (the Ramak), one of the greatest kabbalists of Safed, and edited "Pardes Rimonim," "Sefer HaGerushin" and "Shiur Komah."[1]
His editorial work always included the addition of thematic indexes, the correction of printing errors according to manuscripts, and the addition of explanatory notes. Among the books he edited are:
The books of Abravanel: "Mashmia Yeshua," "Yeshuot Meshiho" and "Ma'aynei HaYeshua," books dealing with matters of the Redemption and the Messiah.[1]
The books of the Radbaz: "Keter Malkhut," "Magen David" and "Metzudat David."[1]
The writings of Rabbi Naftali Hirz Wessely (RaNaHaV): despite the historical controversy surrounding his personality, Rabbi Tzuriel chose to edit his Torah books, such as "Yein Levanon" and "Gan Na'ul," out of recognition of their great value for study.[1]
Books of early kabbalists: "Avodat HaKodesh" by Rabbi Meir ibn Gabbai and "Tuv HaAretz" by Rabbi Natan Shapira.[1]
The choice to edit books dealing with the Redemption (Abravanel) and with Kabbalah (the Ramak) is not accidental. Rabbi Tzuriel believed that in our generation, the generation of Redemption, there is a need to reveal the "soul" of the Torah, and this is done both through the teaching of Rav Kook and through the early sources on which it relied.[1, 6]
Chapter 7: His Attitude to the Land of Israel and Its Commandments
Love of the Land of Israel was a central axis of Rabbi Tzuriel's life and work. His book "Derishat Tziyon" deals with love of the Land and the commandment of settling it, following the order of the weekly Torah portions, and gathers sources from all the generations of Torah that strengthen the bond between the people of Israel and its land.[1] He stressed the virtue of living in the Land and the halakhic and moral duty to work for its upbuilding.[2, 11]
His many essays, published in various forums such as "BeNativ HaChalav" and "Sha'alei Da'at," dealt with topical issues such as self-sacrifice for the conquest of the Land, the halakhic status of the Temple Mount, and the importance of military service.[11] He saw the Israeli soldier as a figure fulfilling a divine mission, and wrote special words of encouragement for the "home-front soldier" in times of war.[11] His son, Rabbi Avraham Tzuriel, who serves as the rabbi of Ness Ziona, is a direct continuation of this line of a rabbinate connected to the whole of Israel and to the life of the State.[2]
Rabbi Tzuriel did not refrain from expressing firm opinions on sensitive issues as well. He strongly opposed any concession of territory of the Land of Israel and saw it as an assault on the foundations of faith.[11] At the same time, his style was always respectful and to the point, based on halakhic and conceptual sources, which enabled him to maintain contact and esteem even among circles that did not agree with his political positions.[2, 7]
Chapter 8: The Educational Legacy and His Influence on His Students
Rabbi Tzuriel's figure as an educator was characterized by a deep connection with every student, regardless of his level of Torah learning or the background he came from. His students describe a feeling of "a son with his father."[10] He would devote hours to personal conversations, answer questions in writing and orally, and encourage young people to write and to produce original Torah insights.[5, 7] Rabbi Harel Dvir relates how Rabbi Tzuriel encouraged him to print his books, quoting the Gemara "His forefathers left him a place in which to distinguish himself," an expression of the rabbi's belief that every learner has a unique portion in the Torah that he must uncover.[5]
His classes were a model of order and clarity. He used to come to Yeshivat Torat HaChaim as a volunteer, sit in the beit midrash and answer questions, and afterwards give a time-limited class on the aggadot of the Sages.[5] His famous alacrity was expressed here too: he would move between subjects and between books quickly, but always made sure that the students understood the bottom line and its practical implication for their service of God.[2]
List of Main Topics in His Recorded Classes (More than 225 Classes)
Chapter 9: His Halakhic and Torah Figure in the Eyes of His Colleagues
Although his fame came chiefly from the world of thought and anthology, Rabbi Tzuriel was an outstanding Torah scholar in the fields of halakha and talmudic analysis as well. His studies at the Chazon Ish Kollel gave him the "seal of quality" of a Lithuanian scholar, and he won great esteem from the Torah giants of Bnei Brak.[2] Former Knesset member Rabbi Dr. Michael Ben-Ari described him as "one of the greatest of the world in scholarship, in kindness and in national pride."[7]
His halakhic ability is expressed in his books "Sho'el U-Meshiv" (short answers to topical questions) and "Beit Yechezkel," which collects laws arranged according to the sanctity of the limbs.[1] He did not hesitate to deal with complex halakhic issues connected with national building, such as the laws of war, the commandment of settling the Land in the present time, and religious-secular relations.[11] His halakhic outlook was always broad, one that seeks to find the "life" within the dry law, in the spirit of Rav Kook's teaching.[2, 7]
Rabbi Tzuriel Halamish of Har Bracha stressed the rabbi's "tremendously radiant countenance" and his vitality, which stayed with him until the age of 85.[7] Even in his last days, while coping with a serious illness, he continued to write, to answer those who asked him, and to bless everyone who turned to him in warm and encouraging handwriting.[5, 7] His blessings were known to be full of generosity of spirit and of faith in the strengths of every Jew.[7]
Summary and Conclusions: The Imprint of Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel
The Torah enterprise of Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel is living testimony to the ability to connect worlds that sometimes seem far apart. He proved that Lithuanian erudition can dwell together with kabbalistic depth, and that personal modesty and asceticism can be combined with extensive public activity and national pride.[2, 7]
The key points of his contribution for the generations:
Making knowledge accessible: creating a human, written "search engine" for the world of Jewish thought through the "treasuries" series.[3, 6]
Systematizing Rav Kook's teaching: turning Rav Kook's expansive thought into an orderly body of teaching accessible to every learner.[6, 8]
Reviving mussar and aggadah: returning the center of gravity of yeshiva study to the refinement of character traits and to the depth of the Sages' words in aggadah.[1, 9]
Connecting faith and reality: demonstrating the link between the wonders of nature (the human body) and the wisdom of the Creator, and between halakha and the national revival in the Land of Israel.[1, 11]
An ideal figure of an educator: a combination of supreme diligence, extreme humility and unconditional love of students.[2, 10]
Rabbi Moshe Tzuriel passed away leaving behind him an entire library that is an enduring treasure for anyone who seeks to delve deeply into the Torah of Israel.[2] His enterprise continues to resonate through his dozens of books, his recorded classes and his many students who continue in his unique path: a path of diligence, truth, love of Israel and constant search for the "treasures of the Torah" hidden in every corner of Jewish thought.[4, 5]
